pages.text: Anti-Defection Law

Anti-Defection Law

• Seven AAP Rajya Sabha MPs, including Raghav
  Chadha and Harbhajan Singh, joined the BJP on April 24, 2026,
  reducing AAP’s Upper House strength from ten to just three members.

• The defection has triggered a legal debate under the Tenth
  Schedule, with no immediate clarity on whether the MPs will face
  disqualification proceedings.

• AAP leader Sanjay Singh announced the party will write to the Rajya
  Sabha Chairman demanding disqualification of the defecting MPs,
  calling the move “unconstitutional”.

Anti-Defection Law


What is Anti Defection? –

• The Tenth Schedule of the Constitution, added by the 52nd
Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985, deals with the
disqualification of MPs and MLAs on grounds of defection.

• It is popularly known as the “Anti-Defection Law” and was
enacted to bring political stability and discourage legislators from
switching parties for personal gain.

• Articles 102(2) and 191(2) of the Constitution state that a
person shall be disqualified from being a member of either House of
Parliament or State Legislature if disqualified under the Tenth
Schedule.

Anti-Defection Law



• The law punishes individual MPs/MLAs who voluntarily leave
their political party or vote against its official stance in the
legislature.

• The main objective was to prevent frequent party-hopping,
which was destabilizing governments — especially after the 1967
general elections, when several state governments were toppled.

• The law applies to both Parliament and State Assemblies, and
it disqualifies elected members for defection to another political
party.

Anti-Defection Law


• The 1985 version of the law allowed a defection to be considered
a "merger" if one-third of the elected members of a political party
broke away together. However, the 91st Constitutional
Amendment Act, 2003, amended this.

• The law does not penalize political parties for accepting or
encouraging defecting legislators, only the individual legislators
are punished.

• The presiding officer (Speaker or Chairman) of the respective
House decides on disqualification cases under the anti-defection law,
but their decision is subject to judicial review.

Anti-Defection Law



• A person who is disqualified under this law can still contest
elections again from any political party for a seat in the same
House.

• Independent legislators come under the law if they join a
political party after being elected. For instance, Jignesh
Mevani (2021) would have been disqualified had he formally joined
the Congress.

• A legislator who disagrees with their party's leadership or
votes against the party line can face disqualification
proceedings under this law.

Anti-Defection Law



• Nominated legislators are allowed to join a political party only
within six months of their nomination. After this period, joining a
party can lead to disqualification.

• According to the law, if the presiding officer finds that a legislator
has violated the provisions of the Tenth Schedule, they lose
their seat in the legislature.

• The constitutional amendment bill's stated purpose was to
curb the “evil of political defections”, which were seen as a
threat to India’s democracy and its core principles.

Anti-Defection Law


History of the law –

• In post-Independence India, frequent defections by legislators
caused major political instability, shaking the foundations of
coalition and single-party governments alike.

• The phrase “Aaya Ram, Gaya Ram” became popular in the late
1960s, after a Haryana MLA switched parties multiple times in a
single day, symbolizing the absurd level of party-hopping.

• Between 1951 and 1967, a total of 542 MLAs changed
parties, showing how common defections had become in the early
decades of Indian democracy.

Anti-Defection Law


• In just one year — between February 1967 and March 1968 —
there were 438 defections, sparking nationwide concern about
political horse-trading and instability.

• These events were documented in the 1968 Y.B. Chavan
Committee report, which was created after a resolution in Lok
Sabha to investigate and suggest solutions.

• A dissent note by CPI leader Bhupesh Gupta explained that
before 1967, defections favoured the Congress, but after its
electoral decline, defections also began hurting the Congress.

Anti-Defection Law



• The Chavan Committee highlighted that the “lure of office”
and money played a major role in defections. After the 1967
elections, 116 out of 210 defectors became ministers in newly
formed governments.

• India follows the Westminster model, where the government
must maintain the majority support of the legislature, creating
pressure on parties to win elections and retain unity post-formation.

• This system made it necessary for political parties to either
secure a majority or build coalitions and prevent their
legislators from defecting, which could bring down their
governments.

Anti-Defection Law



• After the defection crisis of 1967, parties across the spectrum
agreed on the need for legal control over defections, as they
were destabilizing both state and national governments.

• In the 1970s, both the Congress and Janata Party tried but
failed to bring anti-defection legislation due to political hurdles and
lack of parliamentary strength.

• The real breakthrough came with the 52nd Constitutional
Amendment Act, 1985, passed by the Rajiv Gandhi-led
Congress government, which had over 400 MPs in Lok Sabha.

Anti-Defection Law



• This amendment introduced the Tenth Schedule of the
Constitution, formally known as the Anti-Defection Law, aimed at
preventing political defections for personal gain.

• Initially, the law allowed two types of group defections
without penalty:
➢ (a) One-third of legislators splitting from the original party;
➢ (b) Two-thirds merging with another party.

• After the 2003 amendment, only the two-thirds merger
clause remains valid for avoiding disqualification.

Anti-Defection Law


What was 91st amendment?

• The 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003 limited the
size of the Council of Ministers to 15% of the total strength of the
Lok Sabha or State Legislative Assembly, with a minimum of
12 ministers in a state.

• It disqualifies any member disqualified due to defection from
becoming a minister in the Union or State Council of Ministers.

• Such disqualified members also cannot hold any remunerative
political post, ensuring they do not gain benefits through unethical
political shifts.

Anti-Defection Law



• The amendment abolished the provision that allowed a one-
third split in a party without disqualification, which had been
misused to destabilize governments.

• Merger became the only valid exception to disqualification: at
least two-thirds of the party’s legislators must agree to merge with
another party.

• This change was made to curb frequent political defections
and the instability they caused in both Parliament and State
Assemblies.

Anti-Defection Law

Grounds for Defection –

Grounds for Disqualification under the Anti-Defection Law:

➢ If an elected member voluntarily gives up the membership
  of their political party.
➢ If a member votes or abstains from voting in the House
  against the party whip or any official direction issued by their
  political party.
➢ If an independent elected member (not affiliated with any
  party at the time of election) joins a political party after
  getting elected.
➢ If a nominated member of a legislature joins a political
  party after six months from the date of nomination.

Anti-Defection Law



➢ The decision on disqualification is made by the Speaker
  (Lok Sabha/State Assembly) or Chairman (Rajya
  Sabha/Legislative Council) of the respective House.

➢ The decision of the presiding officer is final, though it is
  subject to judicial review by courts.

➢ All such proceedings are treated as proceedings of Parliament
  or the State Legislature, as applicable.

Anti-Defection Law


Exceptions under the law –

• Merger Provision: If two-thirds of the members of a political
party agree to merge with another political party:
   ➢ They will not face disqualification.
   ➢ Members who choose to stay with the original party are also
      not disqualified.

• Speaker/Chairman Exception:
   ➢ If a member is elected as Speaker or Chairman, they can
     resign from their political party without disqualification.
   ➢ They are allowed to rejoin their party after leaving the
     Speaker/Chairman post.

Anti-Defection Law



Splits Not Allowed Anymore:

  ➢ Earlier, a one-third split in a party was considered a valid
    ground for exemption from disqualification.
  ➢ The 91st Constitutional Amendment (2003) removed
    this provision, so splits are now disallowed.

Anti-Defection Law

Problems of Applicability –

• “Voluntarily giving up membership” is not defined, allowing
the Speaker to interpret it arbitrarily — as seen in Ravi S. Naik v.
Union of India (1994), where even speeches and conduct were
considered proof of defection.

• The term “original political party” is ambiguous — whether it
refers to the national, state, or local unit is unclear, complicating
disqualification rulings.

• Speakers often act with political bias, since they belong to a
party and hold discretionary powers, raising concerns about
impartiality — a concern highlighted in Kihoto Hollohan v.
Zachillhu (1992).

Anti-Defection Law



• There is no time limit for the Speaker to decide on
disqualification petitions, enabling deliberate delays for political
benefit — as seen in Manoj Narula v. Union of India (2014).

• The two-thirds merger clause allows mass defections
without disqualification, even if there’s no actual party merger,
undermining the purpose of the law.

• The law punishes individual dissent (“retail defection”) but
protects group defections (“wholesale defection”), creating a
double standard.

Anti-Defection Law


• 91st Constitutional Amendment (2003) removed protection
for party splits but retained protection for mergers, inadvertently
encouraging bulk defections.

• Independent legislators must join a party after election or
face disqualification if they vote differently, limiting their
independence.

• The law discourages free speech and conscience of legislators
by forcing them to follow party whips on all matters, even if they
disagree.

Anti-Defection Law



• Judicial review is limited before the Speaker makes a decision,
delaying remedies even in clear-cut cases — creating a
constitutional grey area.

• Political parties misuse the “merger” route by engineering
defections through inducements and then claiming exemption under
the law.

• Resignation loophole: Legislators resign before defecting,
reduce quorum, and recontest on another ticket — as seen in the
Karnataka crisis of 2019.

Anti-Defection Law



• The law undermines voter representation by prioritizing party
loyalty over constituency interest — turning elected representatives
into party agents.

• Whips are issued even for non-confidence matters, where
individual judgment should matter — reducing Parliament to a
rubber stamp for party decisions.

Anti-Defection Law


Issues with speaker’s role –

• Speakers often act in a partisan manner, favouring their own
political parties during defection cases.

• The office of the Speaker, meant to be neutral, gets dragged into
political controversies due to biased disqualification decisions.

• In 1987, the Speaker of the Tamil Nadu Assembly disqualified
AIADMK members supporting the rival faction, showing selective
application.

Anti-Defection Law



• Delays in deciding petitions are common, as seen in Andhra
Pradesh, Telangana, and Manipur, allowing defectors to
continue in office.

• The Constitution does not prescribe a fixed timeline for Speakers to
decide on disqualification, giving them unchecked discretion.

• In Manipur (2017), the Speaker failed to disqualify a defector for
three years, and only acted after the Supreme Court’s
intervention.

Anti-Defection Law



• Since Speakers are active party members, they face a conflict of
interest between constitutional responsibilities and political loyalties.

• Biased decisions from Speakers erode public faith in democratic
institutions and legislative fairness.

• The Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990) recommended giving
disqualification powers to an independent authority to avoid such
conflicts.

Anti-Defection Law



• Political parties misuse the anti-defection law through loyal
Speakers to protect or punish members as per political needs.

• This manipulation has distorted the original purpose of the anti-
defection law, which was to bring stability and curb unethical
switching.

• There’s little incentive for parties to reform the law or
Speaker’s powers, since they benefit from the existing arrangement.
Overall, the Speaker’s role in anti-defection cases has become a tool
for political manoeuvring, failing to ensure justice or uphold
constitutional morality.

Anti-Defection Law
Recent News –

• In AAP’s case, seven out of ten Rajya Sabha MPs (exactly two-thirds)
  joined the BJP, potentially allowing them to claim protection under this
  clause.

• The Tenth Schedule's merger exception protects defectors if two-
  thirds of a party's members in a House defect together, treating it as a
  valid "merger" rather than defection.

• If the merger exception is accepted, the defecting MPs will not lose
  their Rajya Sabha seats, effectively switching allegiance without legal
  penalty.

Mahanadi River Dispute


• On April 20, 2026, the Mahanadi Water Dispute Tribunal (MWDT) issued
  a warning to Odisha and Chhattisgarh, giving them a last opportunity
  until May 2, 2026, to finalize a consensual settlement formula.


• The tribunal, chaired by former Supreme Court judge Justice Bela M.
  Trivedi, expressed displeasure over repeated adjournments and the
  failure to place any concrete proposal on record.


• If the states fail to submit a consensus by the next hearing, the tribunal
  has made it clear that it will proceed to adjudicate the decade-long
  dispute on its merits without further delay.

Mahanadi River Dispute

The Mahanadi River –
• The Mahanadi originates in Chhattisgarh’s Dhamtari district and
  flows 857 kms before entering Odisha, finally draining into the Bay of
  Bengal.

• The river sustains irrigation (2.35 lakh hectares), hydropower (347.5
  MW), and fisheries across at least 20 of Odisha’s 30 districts.

• The Mahanadi has a total catchment area of 1,41,600 sq km, of
  which 53.9% lies in Chhattisgarh, 45.73% in Odisha, and a
  small portion in Madhya Pradesh.

Mahanadi River Dispute

• The current conflict began in 2016 when Odisha accused Chhattisgarh
  of “unilaterally constructing” at least eight barrages along the
  river.

• Odisha, as the lower riparian state, alleged that these upstream
  projects severely impacted water flow into Odisha, particularly during
  the non-monsoon seasons.

• In response, the Union government attempted to resolve the issue
  through a tripartite meeting with then Chief Ministers Naveen
  Patnaik (Odisha) and Raman Singh (Chhattisgarh), chaired by
  Union Minister Uma Bharti.

Mahanadi River Dispute


• Odisha’s Argument: The river is a lifeline for its agriculture, power
  generation, and fisheries. Odisha maintains that its historical use and the
  ecological needs of the delta give it a primary claim to the water.


• Chhattisgarh’s Argument: As the upper riparian state with over 86%
  of the catchment area up to the Hirakud dam, it argues it has every right to
  use the river's water for its own industrial and economic development.

• Chhattisgarh further points out that of the 35,308 MCM contributed to
  the Hirakud dam, it is currently using only 9,000 MCM, arguing it has the
  right to utilize more.

Mahanadi River Dispute


• Six biodiversity hotspots, including Bhitarkanika, Chilika, and
  Tikarpada, depend on the river’s flows, making the dispute also an
  ecological matter of national importance.

• The dispute has a direct economic impact, as the Mahanadi is critical
  for irrigation, industry, and power generation. The basin contributes
  nearly 40-45% of India’s industrial steel production.

Mahanadi River Dispute

Constitutional Provisions –
• Article 262(1) of the Constitution empowers Parliament to provide
  by law for the adjudication of disputes relating to the use,
  distribution, or control of waters of inter-state rivers or river valleys.

• Article 262(2) allows Parliament to provide that neither the
  Supreme Court nor any other court shall exercise jurisdiction in
  respect of any such dispute, thus potentially excluding the apex
  court’s jurisdiction.

• The Inter-State River Water Disputes Act (ISRWD), 1956,
  was enacted under Article 262 to create a dispute resolution
  mechanism.

Mahanadi River Dispute

ISRWD Act, 1956 –
• Under this Act, when a state government makes a complaint regarding
  a water dispute and the central government believes the dispute
  cannot be settled by negotiations, a Water Disputes Tribunal is
  constituted to adjudicate the matter.

• The Act provides that the decision of the tribunal, after being
  published in the official gazette, shall have the same force as an
  order or decree of the Supreme Court.

• The Act’s provision for creating a separate tribunal for each dispute
  has caused major delays, leading to widespread demands for reform.

Mahanadi River Dispute

National Interlinking of Rivers Project (NRLP) –
• It was formulated in August 1980 to transfer water from surplus
  basins to deficit/deficit basins to mitigate floods and droughts.

• The National Water Development Agency (NWDA) was
  established in 1982 under the Ministry of Jal Shakti to study the
  feasibility of inter-basin water transfer.
• As of 2025, out of the 30 identified links, Pr
• e-Feasibility Reports (PFRs) are complete for all 30 projects, Feasibility
  Reports (FRs) for 26, and Detailed Project Reports (DPRs) for 13 link
  projects.

Mahanadi River Dispute


• The 30 links are divided into two major components: the Himalayan
  Component (14 links) connecting the Ganga-Brahmaputra-Meghna
  system, and the Peninsular Component (16 links) for links
  connecting rivers like Mahanadi, Godavari, and Cauvery.


• Five links have been designated as national priority projects: Ken-Betwa
  Link (KBLP), Modified Parbati-Kalisindh-Chambal (PKC), and a three-part
  Godavari-Cauvery Link.


• The Ken-Betwa Link Project (KBLP) is the first under implementation,
  approved in December 2021 with an estimated cost of ₹44,605 crore,
  targeted for completion by 2030.

Mahanadi River Dispute

Background of the Mahanadi dispute –
• In December 2016, the Odisha government bypassed the tribunal
  route and directly moved the Supreme Court by filing an original suit
  under Article 131 of the Constitution.

• Article 131 grants the Supreme Court exclusive original jurisdiction
  over disputes between the Government of India and one or more
  states, or between two or more states.

• Odisha’s suit sought an injunction against Chhattisgarh to prevent it
  from constructing further barrages along the river.

Mahanadi River Dispute

• Following the Supreme Court’s directive in January 2018, the Centre
  constituted the Mahanadi Water Disputes Tribunal on March 12,
  2018, under the ISRWD Act, 1956.

• The tribunal is currently composed of Justice Bela M. Trivedi
  (Chairperson), along with members Justice Ravi Ranjan and
  Justice Indermeet Kaur Kochhar.

• The Commission has powers equivalent to a civil court for
  summoning witnesses and requiring the production of documents, and
  the tribunal’s term has been extended by nine months, pushing its
  new deadline to January 13, 2027.

Mahanadi River Dispute

• The 2017 Amendment Bill proposed to replace the provision for
  separate tribunals with a single, permanent Inter-State River
  Water Disputes Tribunal, with multiple benches for each dispute to
  speed up adjudication.

• It introduced a Disputes Resolution Committee (DRC) for
  amicable resolution before the matter goes to the tribunal, to be given
  one year (extendable by six months) to submit its report.

• The Bill also reduced the time limit for the tribunal to give its decision
  from three to two years (extendable by one year). However, it
  remains pending in Parliament.

Mahanadi River Dispute

Recent Warning –

• In its April 20 order, the tribunal made it clear that it is “not very
  happy with the manner” in which the proceedings are being
  conducted.
• The bench noted that despite multiple technical committee meetings,
  the states have failed to submit any “concrete proposal for
  settlement on any of the disputed issues”.
• The tribunal observed that the proceedings are being adjourned at the
  order of the parties on the ground that they are “seriously considering
  settlement,” but nothing substantial has materialized.

Mahanadi River Dispute


• On April 11, both states had jointly submitted that the minutes of a
  crucial technical meeting regarding “annual water availability in mean
  annual flow” held on April 8 would be finalized by April 20.

• On the deadline, the respective Advocate Generals again sought more
  time, claiming the meeting data was “crucial”, prompting the tribunal
  to issue its final warning.

• The tribunal fixed May 2, 2026, as the next date of hearing, warning
  that this would be the last opportunity to place a consensus on record.

Mahanadi River Dispute


• The states had submitted a joint request to the Centre, leading to an
  extension of the tribunal’s tenure by nine months till January 13,
  2027.
• The Odisha government formed a high-level committee headed by
  Deputy CM K V Singh Deo, and officials from both states have held
  multiple meetings.
• The tribunal noted that although there are plans by Odisha and
  Chhattisgarh to hold a chief ministers’ meeting to resolve the dispute
  amicably, no consensus has been reached yet.

Mahanadi River Dispute


• The tribunal has made its position clear: if no consensus is placed on
  record by May 2, it will proceed to hear the references on the
  case’s merits and adjudicate the dispute on its own.

• The tribunal’s bench has the authority to frame issues, hear
  arguments, and pass a final, binding award that applies to the sharing
  of the Mahanadi waters.

• If the tribunal adjudicates, it may be years before a final decision
  is implemented, as tribunal awards are often challenged and
  litigated further.
